claim: Malfunction of the CFTR protein results in cystic fibrosis, one of the most common hereditary diseases.
source: Malfunction of the CFTR protein results in cystic fibrosis, one of the most common hereditary diseases.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the scientific literature about CFTR and cystic fibrosis.

claim: CFTR functions as an anion channel, the gating of which is controlled by long-range allosteric communications.
source: CFTR functions as an anion channel, the gating of which is controlled by long-range allosteric communications.
evidence: This statement is supported by established knowledge about CFTR function.

claim: The most effective CFTR drugs modulate its activity allosterically.
source: the most effective CFTR drugs modulate its activity allosterically.
evidence: This is supported by knowledge of current CFTR therapeutics and their mechanisms.

claim: The study integrated Gaussian network model, transfer entropy, and anisotropic normal mode-Langevin dynamics to investigate the allosteric communications network of CFTR.
source: Herein, we integrated Gaussian network model, transfer entropy, and anisotropic normal mode-Langevin dynamics and investigated the allosteric communications network of CFTR.
evidence: This describes the computational methods used in the study.

claim: The computational results are in remarkable agreement with experimental observations and mutational analysis.
source: The results are in remarkable agreement with experimental observations and mutational analysis and provide extensive novel insight.
evidence: This is supported by comparisons made throughout the manuscript between computational predictions and experimental data.

claim: The study identified residues that serve as pivotal allosteric sources and transducers, many of which correspond to disease-causing mutations.
source: We identified residues that serve as pivotal allosteric sources and transducers, many of which correspond to disease-causing mutations.
evidence: This is supported by the GNM-TE analysis and comparison with disease-causing mutations shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6.

claim: In the ATP-free form, dynamic fluctuations of the residues that comprise the ATP-binding sites facilitate the initial binding of the nucleotide.
source: We find that in the ATP-free form, dynamic fluctuations of the residues that comprise the ATP-binding sites facilitate the initial binding of the nucleotide.
evidence: This is inferred from the GNM-TE analysis showing allosteric peaks near ATP-binding sites in the ATP-free state.

claim: Binding of ATP brings to the fore and focuses on dynamic fluctuations that were present in a latent and diffuse form in the absence of ATP.
source: Subsequent binding of ATP then brings to the fore and focuses on dynamic fluctuations that were present in a latent and diffuse form in the absence of ATP.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of GNM-TE results between ATP-free and ATP-bound states shown in Figures 1-3.

claim: Drugs that potentiate CFTR's conductance do so not by directly acting on the gating residues, but rather by mimicking the allosteric signal sent by the ATP-binding sites.
source: We demonstrate that drugs that potentiate CFTR's conductance do so not by directly acting on the gating residues, but rather by mimicking the allosteric signal sent by the ATP-binding sites.
evidence: This is supported by the GNM-TE analysis of ivacaftor-bound CFTR shown in Figure 6.

claim: The study uncovered a previously undiscovered allosteric 'hotspot' located proximal to the docking site of the phosphorylated regulatory (R) domain.
source: We have also uncovered a previously undiscovered allosteric 'hotspot' located proximal to the docking site of the phosphorylated regulatory (R) domain, thereby establishing a molecular foundation for its phosphorylation-dependent excitatory role.
evidence: This is supported by the GNM-TE analysis shown in Figure 3C-D.

claim: Cystic fibrosis affects approximately 1 in every 3000 newborns.
source: It stands as one of the prevailing hereditary afflictions, affecting approximately 1 in every 3000 newborns (Farrell, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Farrell, 2008.

claim: Individuals with CF continue to endure pronounced morbidity and a reduced life expectancy despite significant advancements in therapeutic interventions.
source: Notwithstanding the significant advancements in therapeutic interventions, individuals with CF continue to endure pronounced morbidity and a reduced life expectancy (McBennett et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McBennett et al., 2022.

claim: Most CF patients carry a deletion of Phe 508 in nucleotide binding domain (NBD)1 which leads to protein instability and premature degradation.
source: Most CF patients carry a deletion of Phe 508 in nucleotide binding domain (NBD)1 which leads to protein instability and premature degradation.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the most common CF mutation.

claim: More than 2000 disease-associated mutations in CFTR have been documented.
source: More than 2000 other disease-associated mutations have been documented (Cftr2.org, 2011), many of which remain uncharacterized.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the CFTR2 database.

claim: CFTR functions as a chloride channel, the excretion of which is important for mucus hydration.
source: CFTR functions as a chloride channel, the excretion of which is important for mucus hydration.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR function.

claim: Malfunction of CFTR leads to mucus dehydration and a subsequent decrease in mucus clearance.
source: Malfunction of CFTR leads to mucus dehydration and a subsequent decrease in mucus clearance.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CF pathophysiology.

claim: The over-accumulation of mucus leads to persistent bacterial infections, chronic inflammations, and to organ failure.
source: The over-accumulation of mucus leads to persistent bacterial infections, chronic inflammations, and to organ failure (Fahy and Dickey, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fahy and Dickey, 2010.

claim: CFTR is a member of the ABC transporter protein family, considered to be one of the largest protein families of any proteome.
source: CFTR is a member of the ABC transporter protein family, considered to be one of the largest protein families of any proteome (Dean et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dean et al., 2001.

claim: CFTR is a unique family member, as all other ABC transporters function as active pumps, moving biomolecules against their concentration gradients.
source: CFTR is a unique family member, as all other ABC transporters function as active pumps, moving biomolecules against their concentration gradients (Rees et al., 2009; Gadsby et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rees et al., 2009 and Gadsby et al., 2006.

claim: The domain organization of CFTR is similar to that of canonical ABC transporters, comprising two transmembrane domains (TMDs) and two cytosolic NBDs.
source: The domain organization of CFTR is similar to that of canonical ABC transporters, comprising two transmembrane domains (TMDs) and two cytosolic NBDs.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR structure.

claim: The TMDs form the translocation channel and the NBDs control channel opening and closing through processive cycles of ATP binding, hydrolysis, and release.
source: The TMDs form the translocation channel and the NBDs control channel opening and closing through processive cycles of ATP binding, hydrolysis, and release.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ABC transporter function.

claim: A unique feature of CFTR is the regulatory domain (R) which contains multiple phosphorylation sites and connects the two NBDs giving rise to a TMD1-NBD1-R-TMD2-NBD2 topology.
source: A unique feature of CFTR is the regulatory domain (R) which contains multiple phosphorylation sites and connects the two NBDs giving rise to a TMD1-NBD1-R-TMD2-NBD2 topology.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR structure.

claim: In the resting (non-conducting) state, the funnel-shaped pore is inward-facing and is solvent accessible only to the cytoplasm.
source: In the resting (non-conducting) state, the funnel-shaped pore is inward-facing and is solvent accessible only to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR structure in the resting state.

claim: In the resting state, the NBDs are separated, and the R domain is wedged between them, preventing their dimerization.
source: The NBDs are separated, and the R domain is wedged between them, preventing their dimerization (Liu et al., 2017b; Zhang and Chen, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2017b and Zhang and Chen, 2016.

claim: Upon phosphorylation of the R domain by PKA, it disengages from its inhibitory position and shifts aside.
source: Upon phosphorylation of the R domain by PKA, it disengages from its inhibitory position and shifts aside (Picciotto et al., 1992; Tabcharani et al., 1991).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Picciotto et al., 1992 and Tabcharani et al., 1991.

claim: After phosphorylation, the NBDs are free to bind ATP and form a 'head-to-tail' dimer.
source: The NBDs are now free to bind ATP and form a ''head-to-tail'' dimer (Rees et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2018; Mense et al., 2006), with the two ATP molecules sandwiched at composite binding sites formed at the dimer interface.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rees et al., 2009, Zhang et al., 2018, and Mense et al., 2006.

claim: In CFTR, only one of the ATP sites is hydrolysis-competent while the other (termed the degenerate site) can only bind ATP but not hydrolyze it.
source: In CFTR, like in some other ABC transporters, only one of the ATP sites is hydrolysis-competent while the other (termed the degenerate site) can only bind ATP but not hydrolyze it (Hohl et al., 2012; Csanády et al., 2019; Stockner et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hohl et al., 2012, Csanády et al., 2019, and Stockner et al., 2020.

claim: Formation of the NBDs dimer leads to rearrangements of transmembrane gating residues and subsequent channel opening.
source: Formation of the NBDs dimer leads to rearrangements of transmembrane gating residues and subsequent channel opening.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR gating mechanism.

claim: Hydrolysis of ATP at the catalytic site and release of hydrolysis products leads to opening of the NBDs, channel closure, and resetting of the system.
source: Hydrolysis of ATP at the catalytic site and release of hydrolysis products leads to opening of the NBDs, channel closure, and resetting of the system.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CFTR gating mechanism.

claim: The CFTR mechanism bears resemblance to that of bona fide ABC transporters, where ATP binding and hydrolysis at the NBDs drive the conversion of the TMDs between inward- and outward-facing conformations.
source: This mechanism bears resemblance to that of bona fide ABC transporters, where ATP binding and hydrolysis at the NBDs drive the conversion of the TMDs between inward- and outward-facing conformations (Johnson and Chen, 2018; Kim and Chen, 2018; Nguyen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Johnson and Chen, 2018, Kim and Chen, 2018, and Nguyen et al., 2018.

claim: Most proteins and enzymes are allosteric, where ligand binding at one site affects the functional properties of another (often distant) site.
source: It is now broadly recognized that most proteins and enzymes are allosteric, where ligand binding at one site affects the functional properties of another (often distant) site (Kessel and Ben-Tal, 2018; Liu and Nussinov, 2016; Gerek and Ozkan, 2011; Campitelli et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kessel and Ben-Tal, 2018, Liu and Nussinov, 2016, Gerek and Ozkan, 2011, and Campitelli et al., 2020.

claim: According to the KNF model, the protein exists in a single conformation (an inactive one) to which the allosteric ligand binds, inducing a conformational change that leads to the active conformation.
source: According to Koshland, Némethy, and Filmer (KNF model, Koshland et al., 1966), the protein exists in a single conformation (an inactive one) to which the allosteric ligand binds, inducing a conformational change that leads to the active conformation.
evidence: This is a description of the KNF model supported by citation to Koshland et al., 1966.

claim: According to the MWC model, proteins pre-exist in multiple conformation, and the allosteric ligand preferentially binds to the active conformer, leading to a redistribution of the conformational distributions toward the active one.
source: In contrast, Monod, Wyman, and Changeux (MWC model, Monod et al., 1965) introduced the concept of 'conformational selection', according to which proteins pre-exist in multiple conformation, and the allosteric ligand preferentially binds to the active conformer, leading to a redistribution of the conformational distributions toward the active one (Ma et al., 1999).
evidence: This is a description of the MWC model supported by citations to Monod et al., 1965 and Ma et al., 1999.

claim: An alternative allosteric mechanism termed 'dynamic mechanism' exists, where allostery is mediated by changes in dynamic fluctuations around a mean conformation in the absence of a noticeable conformational change.
source: More recently, an alternative allosteric mechanism was demonstrated, termed 'dynamic mechanism' (Motlagh et al., 2014; Nussinov and Tsai, 2015), where allostery is mediated by changes in dynamic fluctuations around a mean conformation in the absence of a noticeable conformational change (Popovych et al., 2006; Tsai et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Motlagh et al., 2014, Nussinov and Tsai, 2015, Popovych et al., 2006, and Tsai et al., 2008.

claim: In CFTR, multiple allosteric mechanisms combine to generate the observed allosteric phenomenon.
source: In some proteins, as we believe is the case of CFTR, multiple allosteric mechanisms combine to generate the observed allosteric phenomenon.
evidence: This is the authors' interpretation based on their computational results.

claim: Long-range allosteric communications are essential to the function of CFTR.
source: There are abundant examples that long-range allosteric communications are essential to the function of CFTR.
evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and citations in the manuscript.

claim: In CFTR, the binding site of ATP and the affected gating residues are separated by 60–70 Å.
source: One such example is the control of channel opening and closing, where the binding site of the effector molecule (ATP) and the affected gating residues are separated by 60–70 Å (Liu et al., 2017b; Zhang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2017b and Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: ATP-dependent dimerization of the NBDs is insufficient for channel opening which additionally depends on an allosteric pathway that connects the NBDs and the channel pore.
source: Very recently, Levring et al. demonstrated that ATP-dependent dimerization of the NBDs is insufficient for channel opening which additionally depends on an allosteric pathway that connects the NBDs and the channel pore (Levring et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Levring et al., 2023.

claim: The allosteric signal in CFTR originates at the NBDs and gradually propagates toward the gating residues along a clear longitudinal protein axis.
source: Based on rate-equilibrium free-energy relationship analysis, Sorum et al. reached similar conclusions, and suggested that this allosteric signal originates at the NBDs and gradually propagates toward the gating residues along a clear longitudinal protein axis (Sorum et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sorum et al., 2015.

claim: Point mutations at the cytosolic loops increase channel open probability by shifting a pre-existing conformational equilibrium toward the ligand bound conducting conformation.
source: Another example of long-range allostery in CFTR is the finding that point mutations at the cytosolic loops increase channel open probability (even in the absence of ATP) by shifting a pre-existing conformational equilibrium toward the ligand bound conducting conformation (Wang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2010.

claim: The potentiator drug ivacaftor and the dual-function modulator elexacaftor do not bind in the proximity of the gating residues yet increase the open probability of the channel.
source: The potentiator drug ivacaftor and the dual-function modulator elexacaftor do not bind in the proximity of the gating residues (Liu et al., 2019; Fiedorczuk and Chen, 2022a) yet increase the open probability (Po) of the channel (Eckford et al., 2012; Shaughnessy et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2019, Fiedorczuk and Chen, 2022a, Eckford et al., 2012, and Shaughnessy et al., 2021.

claim: GNM reduces the complexity of a protein polymer to a network of nodes (representing the main chain α-carbons) connected by springs with a spring constant of unity.
source: GNM reduces the complexity of a protein polymer to a network of nodes (representing the main chain α-carbons) connected by springs with a spring constant of unity.
evidence: This is a description of the GNM method.

claim: GNM assumes force linearity and isotropy of all fluctuations.
source: Further simplifications are the assumptions of force linearity and isotropy of all fluctuations.
evidence: This is a description of the GNM method.

claim: GNM is computationally economical, allowing for rapid analytical derivation of conformational dynamics even of large proteins.
source: On the one hand, GNM is computationally economical, allowing for rapid analytical derivation of conformational dynamics even of large proteins.
evidence: This is a description of the advantages of the GNM method.

claim: GNM proves highly effective in predicting fluctuations around a predefined native state and offers valuable information regarding allosteric communication and causality.
source: GNM proves highly effective in predicting fluctuations around a predefined native state and offers valuable information regarding allosteric communication and causality.
evidence: This is a description of the capabilities of the GNM method.

claim: Due to its reliance on topology, GNM is unsuitable to monitor the conformational transitions from one native state to another.
source: Nevertheless, due to its reliance on topology, GNM is unsuitable to monitor the conformational transitions from one native state to another.
evidence: This is a description of the limitations of the GNM method.

claim: GNM cannot provide any information on side chains dynamics as these are omitted from the model.
source: In addition, GNM cannot provide any information on side chains dynamics as these are omitted from the model.
evidence: This is a description of the limitations of the GNM method.

claim: GNM-based approaches have been very successful in describing global conformational dynamics of proteins.
source: Despite, or because of, its simplicity, GNM-based approaches have been very successful in describing global conformational dynamics of proteins (Yang and Bahar, 2005; Li et al., 2014; Acar et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Yang and Bahar, 2005, Li et al., 2014, and Acar et al., 2020.

claim: Transfer entropy can be used to determine whether two residues are allosterically connected.
source: In the context of proteins' conformational changes, TE can be used to determine whether two residues are allosterically connected (Altintel et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Altintel et al., 2022.

claim: If TEij(τ) > TEji(τ), then the dynamics of residue i affects the dynamics of residue j, representing a causal relationship between residues i and j.
source: If TEij (τ)>TEji (τ), then the dynamics of residue i affects the dynamics of residue j, representing a causal relationship between residues i and j.
evidence: This is a description of how TE is interpreted in the context of protein dynamics.

claim: If a residue transfers information to many other residues in the protein, it is considered as an information source; if it accepts information from much of the protein, it is considered as an information receiver or a 'sink'.
source: If a residue transfers information to many other residues in the protein, it is considered as an information source; if it accepts information from much of the protein, it is considered as an information receiver or a 'sink' (for more details about the correlation between TE and allostery, see Hacisuleyman and Erman, 2017b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hacisuleyman and Erman, 2017b.

claim: GNM-based TE provides a direct measure, at the linear approximation, of causality relations between residues and domains.
source: Unlike simulation trajectory approaches that infer cause-and-effect relations from the observed sequence of events (which may be circumstantial), GNM-based TE provides a direct measure, at the linear approximation, of causality relations between residues and domains.
evidence: This is a description of the advantages of GNM-based TE.

claim: ANM-LD integrates a low-resolution α-carbon-based ANM with stochastic all-atom implicit solvent LD simulations.
source: The novelty of our approach, ANM-LD, is that it integrates a low-resolution α-carbon-based ANM with stochastic all-atom implicit solvent LD simulations (Brünger et al., 1984).
evidence: This is a description of the ANM-LD method with citation to Brünger et al., 1984.

claim: ANM-LD reflects only internal dynamic modes, free of any external bias.
source: ANM-LD reflects only internal dynamic modes, free of any external bias.
evidence: This is a description of the ANM-LD method.

claim: ANM-LD provides experimentally testable predictions, and has been successfully used to compute conformational trajectories of proteins.
source: More importantly, ANM-LD provides experimentally testable predictions, and has been successfully used to compute conformational trajectories of proteins (Acar et al., 2020; Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Acar et al., 2020 and Yang et al., 2018.

claim: GNM-TE calculations on non-phosphorylated ATP-free human CFTR were performed using the 10 slowest GNM 'modes'.
source: First, we performed GNM-TE calculations on non-phosphorylated ATP-free human CFTR (PDB ID 5UAK, Liu et al., 2017b) using the 10 slowest GNM 'modes'.
evidence: This describes the computational methods used in the study.

claim: The 10 slowest modes of CFTR encompass its complete dynamic spectrum.
source: Indeed, Eigenvalue analysis demonstrated that the 10 slowest modes of CFTR encompass its complete dynamic spectrum (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by eigenvalue analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Very similar results were obtained when Rcut of 7 Å was used instead of 10 Å, suggesting that the results are not very sensitive to this parameter.
source: Very similar results were obtained when Rcut of 7 Å was used instead (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that the results are not very sensitive to this parameter.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Of the 60 residues that serve as main allosteric sources, 22 were located within 4 Å of a hinge residue, and this co-localization was highly statistically significant.
source: Of the 60 residues that serve as main allosteric sources, 22 were located within 4 Å of a hinge residue, and this co-localization was highly statistically significant (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Hinge residues likely play an important role in transmitting the strain energy induced by binding of allosteric ligands.
source: This is perhaps not unexpected, as hinge residues likely play an important role in transmitting the strain energy induced by binding of allosteric ligands.
evidence: This is an inference based on the co-localization of allosteric sources and hinge residues.

claim: In ATP-free CFTR, some of the main entropy peaks located in the NBDs are slightly shifted from the ATP-binding residues and correspond to adjacent residues.
source: Interestingly, some of the main entropy peaks (i.e. entropy sources) located in the NBDs are slightly shifted from the ATP-binding residues (Figure 1) and correspond to adjacent residues.
evidence: This is observed in the GNM-TE analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The shift of entropy peaks from ATP-binding residues disappears once ATP is bound, and the entropy source role is transferred from the neighboring residues to the ATP-binding residues themselves.
source: This shift disappears once ATP is bound, and the entropy source role is transferred from the neighboring residues to the ATP-binding residues themselves (see next results section dealing with the effects of ATP binding).
evidence: This is observed by comparing GNM-TE results for ATP-free and ATP-bound states.

claim: Upon removal of the slowest GNM mode, a new cluster of residues that serve as allosteric sources was revealed in the TMDs.
source: Upon removal of the slowest GNM mode, a new cluster of residues that serve as allosteric sources was revealed (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The cluster of residues revealed upon removal of the slowest mode includes the putative gating residues and additional residues that line the ion permeation pathway.
source: These residues, which are distributed roughly symmetrically in the TMDs, include the putative gating residues (e.g. P99, T338, S341, Liu et al., 2017b) and additional residues that line the ion permeation pathway.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and supported by citation to Liu et al., 2017b.

claim: The residues that form the ivacaftor binding site were revealed as entropy sources by removal of the slowest GNM mode.
source: The residues that form the ivacaftor binding site (Liu et al., 2019) were also revealed as entropy sources by removal of the slowest GNM mode (Figure 2B), demonstrating the utility of this approach.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and supported by citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: Removal of the second slowest GNM mode reveals another cluster of TMD residues that serve as entropy sources, comprised solely of residues in TMD1.
source: Removal of the next slowest GNM mode reveals another cluster of TMD residues that serve as entropy/allostery sources. Unlike the above-described symmetric cluster, this cluster is highly asymmetric, and is comprised solely of residues in TMD1 (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The asymmetric cluster of residues revealed by removing the second slowest mode is located at and just above the future site for docking of the regulatory domain.
source: Interestingly, this cluster of residues is located at and just above the future site for docking of the regulatory domain (Bozoky et al., 2013; Chappe et al., 2005 and see also later in Figure 3C–D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C and supported by citations to Bozoky et al., 2013 and Chappe et al., 2005.

claim: Even when the NBDs are completely separated and the composite ATP-binding sites are yet to form, the dynamic infrastructure for nucleotide binding is already present, poised for binding of the ligand.
source: This demonstrates that even when the NBDs are completely separated and the composite ATP-binding sites are yet to form, the dynamic infrastructure for nucleotide binding is already present, poised for binding of the ligand.
evidence: This is inferred from the GNM-TE analysis of ATP-free CFTR showing entropy sources near ATP-binding sites.

claim: The pre-existing dynamic infrastructure likely facilitates ATP binding and will come into full play at a later stage of the conformational change, following phosphorylation and binding of ATP.
source: This pre-existing dynamic infrastructure likely facilitates ATP binding and will come into full play at a later stage of the conformational change, following phosphorylation and binding of ATP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the GNM-TE analysis.

claim: The above analysis revealed two latent entropy hotspots: one surrounding the ion permeation pathway and the other adjacent to the docking site of the regulatory domain.
source: The above analysis revealed two latent entropy hotspots: one surrounding the ion permeation pathway (Figure 2B) and the other adjacent to the docking site of the regulatory domain (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Both latent entropy hotspots were hidden by the more dominant global fluctuations of the protein.
source: Both sites were hidden by the more dominant global fluctuations of the protein (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is shown by comparing Figure 2A with Figures 2B and 2C.

claim: Phosphorylation and binding of ATP greatly rewires the overall allosteric connectivity in CFTR.
source: We observed that phosphorylation and binding of ATP greatly rewires the overall allosteric connectivity in CFTR (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, and compare Figures 1 and 3A)
evidence: This is shown by comparing Figures 1 and 3A and in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: After phosphorylation and ATP binding, residues that serve as entropy sources are found in all the domains (TMD1, NBD1, TMD2, NBD2).
source: residues that serve as entropy sources are now found in all the domains (TMD1, NBD1, TMD2, NBD2)
evidence: This is observed in the GNM-TE analysis of phosphorylated ATP-bound CFTR.

claim: After phosphorylation and ATP binding, the entropy peaks are sharper than those observed for the unphosphorylated ATP-free form, indicating that information is originating from distinct residues/cluster of residues.
source: the entropy peaks are sharp, sharper than those observed for the unphosphorylated ATP-free form (compare Figures 1 and 3A), indicating that information is originating from distinct residues/cluster of residues.
evidence: This is observed by comparing Figures 1 and 3A.

claim: Phosphorylation and binding of ATP focuses the dynamics of CFTR, which pre-existed in a more diffuse manner in the unphosphorylated ATP-free state.
source: This suggests that phosphorylation and binding of ATP focuses the dynamics of CFTR, which pre-existed in a more diffuse manner in the unphosphorylated ATP-free state.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing GNM-TE results for ATP-free and ATP-bound states.

claim: The phosphorylated ATP-bound conformation is the preferred template/target for structure-guided development of allosteric modulators.
source: This observation suggests that this conformation is the preferred template/target for structure-guided development of allosteric modulators.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that ATP binding focuses the dynamics of CFTR.

claim: Upon binding of ATP, the entropy peaks in the NBDs closely match the location of the ATP-binding residues.
source: This offset largely disappears upon binding of ATP, and the entropy peaks in the NBDs now closely match the location of the ATP-binding residues (compare Figures 1 and 3A).
evidence: This is observed by comparing Figures 1 and 3A.

claim: In the phosphorylated ATP-bound state, the residues that serve as main entropy sources in the TMDs are those that surround the ion permeation channel.
source: In the TMDs, the residues that serve as main entropy sources are those that surround the ion permeation channel (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Upon phosphorylation and binding of ATP the gating and pore lining residues assume a more dominant role in allosteric signaling.
source: This means that upon phosphorylation and binding of ATP the gating and pore lining residues assume a more dominant role in allosteric signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the GNM-TE analysis of phosphorylated ATP-bound CFTR.

claim: The transmitting TMD residues in the phosphorylated ATP-bound state were identified as latent entropy sources in the unphosphorylated ATP-free state.
source: Notably, these transmitting TMD residues were identified as latent entropy sources in the unphosphorylated ATP-free state (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is shown by comparing Figure 2B with Figure 3B.

claim: The underlying dynamics in CFTR pre-exist, prior to phosphorylation and ATP binding.
source: This result again highlights that the underlying dynamics in CFTR pre-exist, prior to phosphorylation and ATP binding.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing GNM-TE results for ATP-free and ATP-bound states.

claim: Binding of ATP had a very similar effect in both human and zebrafish CFTR, suggesting that the allosteric effects of ATP binding are robust and conserved.
source: As shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2, binding of ATP had a very similar effect in both CFTR homologues, suggesting that the allosteric effects of ATP binding are robust and conserved.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the phosphorylated ATP-bound state, upon removal of the slowest mode, the entropy sources in the NBDs have migrated from the ATP-binding sites at the dimer interface toward the intracellular loops.
source: First, the entropy sources in the NBDs have now migrated from the ATP-binding sites at the dimer interface toward the intracellular loops, perfectly positioned to transmit the signal to the TMDs.
evidence: This is observed in the GNM-TE analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the phosphorylated ATP-bound state, upon removal of the slowest mode, the TMD allosteric peaks surrounding the gating residues and the ion permeation pathway have migrated toward the extracellular exit.
source: Second, the TMD allosteric peaks surrounding the gating residues and the ion permeation pathway have migrated toward the extracellular exit, as if to prepare for ion exit.
evidence: This is observed in the GNM-TE analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the phosphorylated ATP-bound state, upon removal of the slowest mode, a cluster of residues that serve as strong entropy sources appeared in TMD1 adjacent to the site of interaction of the regulatory (R) domain.
source: Lastly, a cluster of residues that serve as strong entropy sources appeared in the TMDs in an asymmetric manner (Figure 3C–D). These residues are found exclusively in TMD1 and comprise or are adjacent to the site of interaction of the regulatory (R) domain (Bozoky et al., 2013; Chappe et al., 2005).
evidence: This is shown in Figures 3C-D and supported by citations to Bozoky et al., 2013 and Chappe et al., 2005.

claim: The role of the R domain may not be limited to steric obstruction of NBD dimer formation in the unphosphorylated ATP-free state.
source: This observation suggests that the role of the R domain may not be limited to steric obstruction of NBD dimer formation in the unphosphorylated ATP-free state.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of an allosteric cluster near the R domain docking site.

claim: The presence of a cluster of information-transmitting residues in the vicinity of the docking site of the R domain may explain previous observations that deletion of the R domain leads to fewer channel opening events.
source: The presence of this cluster of information-transmitting residues in the vicinity of the docking site of the R domain may explain previous observations that deletion of the R domain leads to fewer channel opening events, and that exogenous addition of the phosphorylated R domain peptide increases channel open probability of CFTR construct deleted of the R domain (Winter and Welsh, 1997; Ma et al., 1997).
evidence: This is inferred from the GNM-TE results and supported by citations to Winter and Welsh, 1997 and Ma et al., 1997.

claim: The 2D cross-correlation map is dominated by large and continuous patches of red (positive correlation) and blue (negative correlation) areas.
source: The map is dominated by large and continuous patches of red (positive correlation) and blue (negative correlation) areas
evidence: This is observed in the cross-correlation map shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The 2D cross-correlation map of CFTR is very similar to that calculated for PglK, a lipid-linked oligosaccharide flippase that adopts the canonical ABC exporter 3D fold.
source: and is very similar to the 2D cross-correlation map calculated for PglK (Acar et al., 2020), a lipid-linked oligosaccharide flippase that adopts the canonical ABC exporter 3D fold (Perez et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Acar et al., 2020 and Perez et al., 2015.

claim: Global rigid body motions with a relatively small number of hinges underlie the conformational change from ATP-free to ATP-bound CFTR.
source: These observations suggest that, as inferred from the cryo-EM structures of CFTR (Liu et al., 2017b; Zhang et al., 2018), global rigid body motions with a relatively small number of hinges underlie this conformational change
evidence: This is inferred from the cross-correlation map and supported by citations to Liu et al., 2017b and Zhang et al., 2018.

claim: The conformational changes of CFTR are similar to those of canonical ABC exporters.
source: and that the conformational changes of CFTR are similar to those of canonical ABC exporters.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity of the cross-correlation map to that of PglK.

claim: The two NBDs display asymmetric allosteric connectivity.
source: The two NBDs display asymmetric allosteric connectivity:
evidence: This is observed in the cross-correlation analysis shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: NBD1 shows a tighter correlation with the residues that surround the permeation pathway.
source: NBD1 shows a tighter correlation with the residues that surround the permeation pathway (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: NBD2 is more strongly correlated with ECL1.
source: while NBD2 (harboring the catalytic Walker B glutamate) is more strongly correlated with ECL1 (extracellular loop 1) (Figure 4C)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4C.

claim: ECL1 is known to stabilize the conducting state of the channel.
source: which is known to stabilize the conducting state of the channel (Infield et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Infield et al., 2016.

claim: Rate-equilibrium free-energy relationship analysis and single molecule FRET studies suggest that the allosteric signal originates at the NBDs and propagates to the TMDs.
source: Rate-equilibrium free-energy relationship analysis and single molecule FRET studies both suggest that the allosteric signal originates at the NBDs and propagates to the TMDs (Sorum et al., 2015; Levring et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sorum et al., 2015 and Levring et al., 2023.

claim: The conformational change from the dephosphorylated ATP-free state to the phosphorylated ATP-bound one begins with the movement of the NBDs.
source: Our results agree with these observations: in parallel simulations we repeatedly observed that the conformational change from the dephosphorylated ATP-free state to the phosphorylated ATP-bound one begins with the movement of the NBDs.
evidence: This is observed in the ANM-LD simulations.

claim: The catalytic NBD2 seems to provide the greater allosteric input.
source: Of the two NBDs, the catalytic NBD2 seems to provide the greater allosteric input (Figure 1 and Figure 2A )
evidence: This is shown in Figures 1 and 2A.

claim: The movement of NBD2 is the leading event and those of ICL2/3, TMD2/TM8, and ECL1 follow.
source: This observation strongly suggests that the movement of NBD2 is the leading event and those of ICL2/3, TMD2/TM8, and ECL1 follow
evidence: This is inferred from the time-delayed cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The allosteric signal propagates from NBD2 to ICL2/3, TMD2/TM8, and ECL1.
source: and that the allosteric signal propagates from NBD2 to ICL2/3, TMD2/TM8, and ECL1 (Figure 5 center, green arrows).
evidence: This is inferred from the time-delayed cross-correlation analysis and shown in Figure 5.

claim: Based on single molecule studies, Levring et al. proposed similar cause-and-effect relations between the catalytic ATP site and TM8.
source: Notably, based on their recent single molecule studies, Levring et al. proposed similar cause-and-effect relations between the catalytic ATP site and TM8 (Levring et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Levring et al., 2023.

claim: From ECL1 the allosteric signal propagates to NBD1.
source: From ECL1 the allosteric signal propagates to NBD1: The movements of these two domains are highly correlated, but only if ECL1 leads and NBD1 follows (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 magenta rectangles, Figure 5 step II, and Figure 5 center, magenta arrow).
evidence: This is inferred from the time-delayed cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5.

claim: From NBD1 the allosteric signal propagates to the gating residues and to the TM helices that surround the permeation pathway.
source: Similar considerations suggest that from NBD1 the allosteric signal propagates to the gating residues and to the TM helices that surround the permeation pathway: The movements of these domains are only synchronized if the former leads and the latter follows (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 blue rectangles, Figure 5 step III, and Figure 5 center, blue arrow).
evidence: This is inferred from the time-delayed cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5.

claim: The movements of the gating residues and the permeation pathway TM helices are correlated with those of NBD2, but only if the TM helices lead and NBD2 follows.
source: In turn, the movements of the gating residues and the permeation pathway TM helices are correlated with those of NBD2, but only if the TM helices lead and NBD2 follows (Figure 5—figure supplement 1 orange rectangles, Figure 5 Step IV).
evidence: This is inferred from the time-delayed cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and Figure 5.

claim: The allosteric signal propagates from the permeation pathway to NBD2, thus completing the cycle of allosteric transduction.
source: We therefore conclude that the allosteric signal propagates from the permeation pathway to NBD2, thus completing the cycle of allosteric transduction (Figure 5 center, orange arrow).
evidence: This is inferred from the time-delayed cross-correlation analysis and shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the past decade, the development of small-molecule CFTR modulators revolutionized CF treatment and led to a dramatic reduction in patient morbidity and increased life expectancy.
source: In the past decade, the development of small-molecule CFTR modulators revolutionized CF treatment and led to a dramatic reduction in patient morbidity and increased life expectancy (Clancy, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Clancy, 2018.

claim: The type I correctors lumacaftor and tezacaftor stabilize mutant CFTR variants, reducing premature protein degradation and improving surface presentation of the mature channel.
source: The type I correctors lumacaftor (VX-809) and tezacaftor (VX-661) stabilize mutant CFTR variants (predominantly the most common ΔF508 mutation) reducing premature protein degradation and improving surface presentation of the mature channel (Van Goor et al., 2011; Fiedorczuk and Chen, 2022b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Van Goor et al., 2011 and Fiedorczuk and Chen, 2022b.

claim: The potentiator ivacaftor enhances the activity of conductance-defective mutants by increasing the open probability of the channel.
source: The potentiator ivacaftor (VX-770) enhances the activity of conductance-defective mutants by increasing the open probability (Po) of the channel (Levring et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2019; Eckford et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to Levring et al., 2023, Liu et al., 2019, and Eckford et al., 2012.

claim: The dual-function type III corrector elexacaftor stabilizes unstable variants and increases channel open probability.
source: and the dual-function type III corrector elexacaftor (VX-445) stabilizes unstable variants and increases channel open probability (Shaughnessy et al., 2021; Veit et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shaughnessy et al., 2021 and Veit et al., 2021.

claim: The type I correctors lumacaftor and tezacaftor bind at 'valleys', i.e., to residues that are not allosteric sources.
source: As shown in Figure 6A, the type I correctors lumacaftor and tezacaftor bind at 'valleys', i.e., to residues that are not allosteric sources.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The results for lumacaftor and tezacaftor are consistent with the mechanism of these drugs which improve the function of CFTR by lowering its ∆G(folding) rather than by modulating its activity.
source: These results are consistent with the mechanism of these drugs which improve the function of CFTR by lowering its ∆G(folding) rather than by modulating its activity (Fiedorczuk and Chen, 2022b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fiedorczuk and Chen, 2022b.

claim: The residues that comprise the binding sites for ivacaftor and elexacaftor include ones that serve as main allosteric sources.
source: In contrast, the residues that comprise the binding sites for ivacaftor and elexacaftor also include ones that serve as main allosteric sources (Figure 6A), alluding to their role as allosteric modulators.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Ivacaftor is used to treat CF patients who carry mutations in the NBDs (most commonly the G551D mutation at the highly conserved LSGGQ ATP binding/signature motif).
source: The potentiator drug ivacaftor is used to treat CF patients who carry mutations in the NBDs (most commonly the G551D mutation at the highly conserved LSGGQ ATP binding/signature motif) (Liu et al., 2019; Eckford et al., 2012; Hadida et al., 2014; Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2019, Eckford et al., 2012, Hadida et al., 2014, and Yu et al., 2012.

claim: Ivacaftor increases channel opening probability despite impaired ATP binding and hydrolysis.
source: Ivacaftor increases channel opening probability despite impaired ATP binding and hydrolysis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about ivacaftor's mechanism.

claim: Ivacaftor does not bind in the vicinity of either the ATP- or ion-coordinating residues but rather peripherally at the protein-lipid interface.
source: The molecular basis for the beneficial effects of ivacaftor is not fully understood, especially since it does not bind in the vicinity of either the ATP- or ion-coordinating residues but rather peripherally at the protein-lipid interface (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: Unlike the folding correcting drugs, ivacaftor does not induce a significant conformational change in ΔF508 CFTR.
source: In addition, unlike the folding correcting drugs, ivacaftor does not induce a significant conformational change in ΔF508 CFTR (Fiedorczuk and Chen, 2022a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Fiedorczuk and Chen, 2022a.

claim: The gating residues and those that line the permeation pathway were not among the residues that receive information from the ivacaftor binding site.
source: Surprisingly, the gating residues and those that line the permeation pathway were not among the residues that receive information from the drug binding site (Figure 6B), leaving the molecular basis of the drug's action unclear.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The ivacaftor docking site and the ATP-binding site send information to a very similar set of residues (Pearson's correlation coefficient of 0.83).
source: As shown in Figure 6C, the two profiles showed remarkable overlap: The ivacaftor docking site and the ATP-binding site send information to a very similar set of residues (Pearson's correlation coefficient of 0.83).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6C and includes a quantitative measure (Pearson's correlation coefficient).

claim: Ivacaftor increases the opening probability not by directly affecting the gating residues but rather indirectly by mimicking the allosteric signaling evoked by ATP binding.
source: These observations suggest that ivacaftor increases the opening probability not by directly affecting the gating residues but rather indirectly by mimicking the allosteric signaling evoked by ATP binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the GNM-TE analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: Ivacaftor exerts its potentiating effect by mimicking the combined allosteric output of the ATP-binding and gating residues, compensating for any potential allosteric transduction short circuit caused by mutations.
source: This result suggests that ivacaftor exerts its potentiating effect by mimicking the combined allosteric output of the ATP-binding and gating residues, compensating for any potential allosteric transduction short circuit caused by mutations.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of allosteric signaling patterns shown in Figure 6.

claim: In the absence of phosphorylation and ATP, CFTR adopts solely the NBDs-open conformation and spontaneous conversions to the NBDs-closed conformation are not seen.
source: In the absence of phosphorylation and ATP, CFTR adopts solely the NBDs-open conformation and spontaneous conversions to the NBDs-closed conformation are not seen (Levring et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Levring et al., 2023.

claim: Multiple phosphorylation events are required to dislodge the R domain from its obstructing position, presenting a very large energetic barrier.
source: In addition, multiple phosphorylation events are required to dislodge the R domain from its obstructing position, presenting a very large energetic barrier (Liu et al., 2017b; Gadsby and Nairn, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Liu et al., 2017b and Gadsby and Nairn, 1999.

claim: The conformational homogeneity of dephosphorylated ATP-free CFTR suggests that the first step of the conformational change, that of movement of the R domain, cannot efficiently proceed via an ensemble selection mechanism.
source: This conformational homogeneity of dephosphorylated ATP-free CFTR suggests that the first step of the conformational change, that of movement of the R domain, cannot efficiently proceed via an ensemble selection mechanism.
evidence: This is inferred from the conformational homogeneity of ATP-free CFTR.

claim: The movement of the R domain occurs by an induced fit mechanism, where the reversible covalent phosphorylation is the allosteric ligand.
source: In the absence of definitive experimental/computational evidence, we currently propose that this step occurs by an induced fit mechanism, where the reversible covalent phosphorylation is the allosteric ligand (Figure 7, step I).
evidence: This is a proposal by the authors based on their analysis, shown in Figure 7.

claim: After phosphorylation the NBDs solely adopt the open conformation and do not spontaneously close unless ATP is added.
source: On the one hand, single molecule studies showed that even after phosphorylation the NBDs solely adopt the open conformation and do not spontaneously close unless ATP is added.
evidence: This is based on single molecule studies.

claim: Once ATP was added, all the molecules converted to the closed-NBD conformation and were never seen to spontaneously open their NBDs.
source: Once ATP was added, all the molecules converted to the closed-NBD conformation and were never seen to spontaneously open their NBDs (Levring et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Levring et al., 2023.

claim: MD simulations showed that the closed state with dimerized NBDs is stable over hundreds of nanoseconds.
source: Along the same lines, MD simulations showed that the closed state with dimerized NBDs is stable over hundreds of nanoseconds (Zeng et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zeng et al., 2023.

claim: Direct experimental evidence supporting an induced fit mechanism for ATP binding was provided by macroscopic current recordings combined with double mutant cycles.
source: Direct experimental evidence supporting an induced fit mechanism was also provided by macroscopic current recordings combined with double mutant cycles (Szollosi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Szollosi et al., 2010.

claim: In the ATP-free form, the ATP-binding residues fluctuate considerably in the absence of nucleotide, sampling conformations in the vicinity of the NBDs-separated native state.
source: This means that the ATP-binding residues fluctuate considerably in the absence of nucleotide, sampling conformations in the vicinity of the NBDs-separated native state.
evidence: This is inferred from the GNM-TE analysis showing allosteric peaks near ATP-binding sites in the ATP-free state.

claim: Some of the conformations sampled by ATP-binding residues in the ATP-free state likely provide an initial state for the interaction with the nucleotide.
source: Some of these conformations likely provide an initial state for the interaction with the nucleotide (Figure 7, step II).
evidence: This is inferred from the GNM-TE analysis and shown in Figure 7.

claim: ATP will selectively bind to conformers that provide an initial state for interaction, as in ensemble selection allosteric mechanism.
source: ATP will selectively bind to these conformers, as in ensemble selection allosteric mechanism.
evidence: This is part of the authors' proposed mechanism.

claim: Once the docking of the nucleotide is initiated by dynamic fluctuations and ensemble selection, closure of the NBDs can proceed by an induced fit mechanism.
source: Once the docking of the nucleotide is initiated by this combination of dynamic fluctuations, ensemble selection closure of the NBDs can proceed by an induced fit mechanism (Figure 7, step III) as suggested by experimental evidence (Szollosi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is part of the authors' proposed mechanism, supported by citation to Szollosi et al., 2010 and shown in Figure 7.

claim: The phosphorylated ATP bound structure observed in the cryo-EM studies is non-conducting: the pore is fully dehydrated, and an ion translocation pathway is missing.
source: The resulting conformational changes do not yet lead to channel opening and conductance: The phosphorylated ATP bound structure observed in the cryo-EM studies is non-conducting: the pore is fully dehydrated, and an ion translocation pathway is missing.
evidence: This is based on cryo-EM structures.

claim: Phosphorylation, ATP binding, and closure of the NBDs are essential yet insufficient for channel opening.
source: Therefore, phosphorylation, ATP binding, and closure of the NBDs are essential yet insufficient for channel opening.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that the ATP-bound structure is non-conducting.

claim: MD simulations of chloride conductance showed that a major conformational change is not required for channel opening. Instead, slight side chain re-orientations of pore residues enable sporadic pulses of chloride conductance.
source: MD simulations of chloride conductance showed that a major conformational change is not required for channel opening. Instead, slight side chain re-orientations of pore residues enable sporadic pulses of chloride conductance (Zeng et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zeng et al., 2023.

claim: Single molecule measurements failed to identify any conformational changes between the conducting and non-conducting states.
source: Single molecule measurements also failed to identify any conformational changes between the conducting and non-conducting states (Levring et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Levring et al., 2023.

claim: Allosteric potentiators that increase CFTR's channel-open probabilities do so without noticeable effects on its conformation.
source: Along the same lines, allosteric potentiators that increase CFTR's channel-open probabilities do so without noticeable effects on its conformation (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: The conformations of the conducting and non-conducting states are very similar and a major conformational change is not required to open the channel.
source: These studies suggest that the conformations of the conducting and non-conducting states are very similar and that a major conformational change is not required to open the channel.
evidence: This is inferred from multiple lines of evidence cited in the manuscript.

claim: Transition to the conducting state occurs by a dynamic allosteric mechanism with rapid conformational sampling around the phosphorylated ATP-bound NBDs-closed state.
source: Rather, transition to the conducting state occurs by a dynamic allosteric mechanism with rapid conformational sampling around the phosphorylated ATP-bound NBDs-closed state (Figure 7, step IV).
evidence: This is part of the authors' proposed mechanism shown in Figure 7.
